method_card.title: Simultaneous Equations (Linear)
steps: Find (or make) a matching pair — the same number in front of x or of y in both equations.
Same signs? Subtract. Opposite signs? Add. The matched letter vanishes.
Solve what's left, substitute back, and check the pair in both equations.
method_card.content:
Simultaneous equations are two equations sharing the same two unknowns. Exactly one pair of values — an \(x\) and a \(y\) — fits both, and your job is to find it by making one letter disappear.

Remember SSS — Same Signs Subtract. Opposite signs? Add instead.
method_card.example:
Solve \(2x + y = 7\) and \(x + y = 4\)

Both have \(+y\) — same signs, so subtract: \(x = 3\). Then \(3 + y = 4\), so \(y = 1\). Check in the first: \(2(3) + 1 = 7\) ✓

gold.hint: No single multiplication works here — scale BOTH equations (try ×3 and ×4, or ×2 and ×3).

misconceptions.message: After scaling by 3 and 4 the right-hand sides are 75 and 72. Subtract them: \(x = 75 - 72 = 3\). Adding them (147) is the slip — the right-hand sides get subtracted just like the left.
Both equations must be multiplied on BOTH sides. Scaling \(2x + 3y = 18\) by 4 gives \(8x + 12y = 72\) — if the 18 is left unscaled, x comes out as 57, which fits neither equation.

gold.hint: Scale both equations — ×4 and ×3 makes both y terms 12y.
Scale both (×2 and ×3 makes both 6y). Negative numbers appear — keep signs on a tight leash.
Scale both equations — ×5 and ×2 makes both y terms 10y.

misconceptions.message: \(x = 3\) is right. Substituting into \(7x + 2y = 27\) gives \(21 + 2y = 27\), so \(2y = 6\) and \(y = 3\). Getting 24 means the 21 was added instead of subtracted when moving it across.

gold.hint: Scale both (×7 and ×3 makes the y terms −21y and +21y) — opposite signs, so add.

misconceptions.message: \(x = 2\) is right. Substituting into \(5x - 3y = 1\) gives \(10 - 3y = 1\), so \(3y = 9\) and \(y = 3\) — positive. Getting \(-3\) means a sign flipped once too often on the way.
misconceptions.note: From 10 - 3y = 1: -3y = -9 so y = 3; the slip keeps y = -3.

bronze.hint: The y terms are +y and −y — opposite signs, so ADD the equations.
Both equations have +y — same sign, so subtract one from the other.

misconceptions.message: When you subtract the equations, the right-hand sides subtract too: \(9 - 5 = 4\), so \(x = 4\). Adding them instead gives 14, which is too big to fit either equation — always do the same thing to both sides.

bronze.hint: Both equations have +y — subtract to make the y terms vanish.

misconceptions.message: Subtracting the left-hand sides means subtracting the right-hand sides as well: \(11 - 5 = 6\), so \(2x = 6\) and \(x = 3\). It looks like the right-hand sides were added instead.

bronze.hint: The x terms already match — subtract to remove them.

misconceptions.message: Subtracting the equations removes x and leaves \(y = 10 - 7 = 3\). It looks like the right-hand sides were added (giving 17) instead of subtracted — both sides get the same treatment.

bronze.hint: Opposite signs on y — adding the equations makes y disappear.

misconceptions.message: Whichever route you take, the right-hand sides must get the same operation as the left. Adding: \(4x = 16\) so \(x = 4\). Subtracting: \(2y = 4\) so \(y = 2\). Mixing the two up leads to \(x = 1, y = 8\), which doesn't fit either equation.
Subtract the right-hand sides too: \(17 - 7 = 10\), so \(2x = 10\) and \(x = 5\). Adding them gives 24 and everything after that comes out wrong.

bronze.hint: The x terms match — subtract to leave just y terms.

misconceptions.message: After subtracting, \(2y = 14 - 6 = 8\), so \(y = 4\). It looks like the right-hand sides were added — they must be subtracted, exactly like the left-hand sides.

bronze.hint: Same sign on y in both — subtract.

misconceptions.message: Subtracting gives \(2x = 13 - 7 = 6\), so \(x = 3\). Adding the right-hand sides (20) instead of subtracting sends the whole answer off course.

silver.hint: Multiply the second equation by 2, then subtract.

misconceptions.message: When you multiply an equation, multiply BOTH sides. \(x + y = 8\) doubled is \(2x + 2y = 16\) — the 8 doubles too. Leaving it as 8 makes every later step wrong.
After doubling the second equation the right-hand sides are 19 and 16, and subtracting gives \(x = 3\). It looks like they were added (35) instead of subtracted.

silver.hint: Multiply the second equation by 2 so both have 2x. Watch out — x comes out negative.

misconceptions.message: Doubling \(x + 2y = 8\) gives \(2x + 4y = 16\) — the right-hand side doubles as well. Keeping it at 8 gives \(y = 13\), which is too big to fit either equation.
Subtract the right-hand sides: \(21 - 16 = 5\), so \(y = 5\). Adding them (37) instead of subtracting is the slip here.

silver.hint: Multiply the first equation by 3 so both have 3y.

misconceptions.message: Multiplying \(4x + y = 14\) by 3 gives \(12x + 3y = 42\) — the 14 gets multiplied too. If the right-hand side stays at 14 you end up with decimals that don't fit the equations.
After scaling, subtract the right-hand sides: \(42 - 12 = 30\), so \(10x = 30\) and \(x = 3\). Adding them (54) is the slip — both sides get subtracted.

silver.hint: Multiply the first equation by 3. The y terms then have opposite signs — so add.

misconceptions.message: \(x = 2\) is right. Substituting into \(5x - y = 5\) gives \(10 - y = 5\), so \(y = 5\) — positive. Getting \(-5\) means the sign flipped once too often when moving terms across.
misconceptions.note: From 10 - y = 5: -y = -5 so y = 5; the slip keeps y = -5.

silver.hint: Multiply the second equation by 2 so both have 4y.

misconceptions.message: Doubling \(3x + 2y = 11\) gives \(6x + 4y = 22\) — the 11 doubles too. Leaving it at 11 makes x come out negative when it shouldn't.
Subtracting the right-hand sides gives \(22 - 17 = 5\), so \(5x = 5\) and \(x = 1\). Adding them (39) instead is the slip here.

silver.hint: Multiply the first equation by 3 so both have 3y.

misconceptions.message: \(x = 3\) is right. Substituting into \(3x + y = 13\) gives \(9 + y = 13\), so \(y = 4\). Getting 22 means the 9 was added to 13 instead of subtracted — moving a term across the equals sign changes its sign.

silver.hint: Multiply the second equation by 3. Opposite signs on the y terms — add.

misconceptions.message: Multiplying \(x + y = 8\) by 3 gives \(3x + 3y = 24\) — the 8 is multiplied too. Keeping it at 8 gives decimal answers, and this question has whole-number ones.

problem_bank.gold_description: Multiply both equations — or switch to the substitution method
problem_bank.bronze_description: The numbers in front already match — add or subtract once and a letter vanishes
problem_bank.silver_description: Multiply one equation first to make a matching pair

steps.label: Step 1 — Spot the match
steps.content: Both equations contain exactly \(+y\) — same sign in both. Same Signs Subtract.

steps.label: Step 2 — Subtract the equations
steps.content: \((3x + y) - (x + y) = 10 - 4\) → \(2x = 6\) → \(x = 3\). The \(y\) terms cancel, and the right-hand sides are subtracted too.

steps.label: Step 1 — Spot the match
steps.content: The \(y\) terms are \(+2y\) and \(-2y\) — same size, opposite signs. Opposite signs means add: \(+2y\) and \(-2y\) make zero.

steps.label: Step 1 — Nothing matches yet
steps.content: \(2x\) vs \(x\), \(3y\) vs \(y\) — no matching pair. Multiply the whole second equation by 3: \(3x + 3y = 15\). The 5 gets multiplied too — every term, both sides.

steps.label: Step 1 — Scale BOTH equations
steps.content: No single multiplication makes a match, so make the \(y\) terms both \(6y\): first equation \(\times 2\) → \(8x + 6y = 46\); second \(\times 3\) → \(9x + 6y = 48\). Both sides of both equations get scaled.

steps.label: Step 1 — Make y the subject
steps.content: From the first equation: \(y = 11 - 2x\). This is the substitution method — the alternative to elimination, and worth the same marks.

steps.label: Step 2 — Substitute into the other equation

bronze.title: Bronze — the pair already matches
steps: You need the one pair of values — an \(x\) AND a \(y\) — that fits both equations. In bronze, a matching pair is already there (like \(+y\) in both).
Same Signs Subtract — subtract one equation from the other (right-hand sides too) and the matched letter vanishes. Opposite signs (\(+y\) and \(-y\))? Add instead.
Solve the one-letter equation that's left, then substitute your value into the easier original equation to find the other letter.

steps.label: Match
steps.content: Both equations have \(+y\) — same sign, so subtract.

silver.title: Silver — make a match first
steps: Now nothing matches yet. Multiply ONE whole equation — every term, both sides of the equals sign — until a pair matches.
Then it's a bronze question: same signs subtract, opposite signs add.
Substitute back and check your pair in both equations.

gold.title: Gold — multiply both equations
steps: Sometimes no single multiplication works. Multiply BOTH equations to hit a common target — \(3y\) and \(2y\) both become \(6y\) with \(\times 2\) and \(\times 3\).
Everything else is the same: same signs subtract, opposite signs add, substitute back, check.
Prefer rearranging? Substitution also works: make \(y\) the subject of one equation and substitute it into the other. Either method gets full marks.
